articles.title: No 'switch' to stop small boats, Lucy Powell tells BBC
articles.summary: Labour's deputy leader was speaking to BBC local radio ahead of the party's annual conference
articles.body:
There is no "switch" to stop small boat crossings, and not every migrant boat can be intercepted, Labour's deputy leader has told the BBC.

Lucy Powell's comments came after two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.

The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, calling the failure to intercept the two boats "not acceptable".

But the Conservatives say Labour has lost control of Britain's borders, and a "radically different" approach is needed.

A total of 781 people were recorded as arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest in a single day for far this year.

In a round of interviews with BBC local radio ahead of Labour's annual conference, Powell told BBC Solent: "We are taking all steps we can to really bear down on and eradicate the small boat crossings altogether.

"This has been a mammoth task across a whole range of different policy areas over the last couple of years, which is now starting to bear fruit, in that small boat crossings are significantly down this year - in fact significantly lower than at any time in the last six years.

"Obviously as we close down some avenues and we close down routes criminal gangs look to find new ways to deliver their terrible business model."

The thousands of migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats.

Before Monday, no small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort had been officially recorded since September 6, 2025.

Uncontrolled landings are so rare that last year's incident was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023.

Powell told BBC Kent: "It's not easy, if we had a switch that we could switch tomorrow to stop all small boats, we would switch it".

Labour's deputy leader and Education Secretary told Radio 4's Today programme that "(You) can't stop everything all of the time.

"Of course, it's a concern. That's why the Home Secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable."

The Conservative Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said on X: "Labour has lost control of our borders.

"A radically different approach is needed.

"We need to leave the ECHR so anyone entering Britain illegally can be rapidly deported. No hotels. No benefits. No lengthy court process. No asylum claim. Just rapid removal. Then the crossings will soon stop."

The Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson MP, said closer cooperation with the EU was key to tacking small boat crossings.

"Until the government adopts Liberal Democrat proposals to tackle the root cause by entering the EU's landmark Migration and Asylum Pact, these the smugglers will continue to find a way through, lives will be put at risk and taxpayers' money will be wasted," he said.

articles.title: Far-right UK activist Daniel Thomas arrested after slashing dinghy
articles.summary: Thomas, 37, arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, endangering the safety of a ship.
articles.body:
British police have arrested a far-right anti-immigration activist after he live-streamed footage appearing to show him slashing an empty dinghy in the English Channel with a knife while a French coastguard official was still on board.

Daniel Thomas, 37, known to his supporters as “Danny Tommo,” was detained on Wednesday evening at a petrol station and remains in custody, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said on Thursday.

He was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, endangering the safety of a ship and offences under the Aviation and Maritime Security Act and the Merchant Shipping Act.

The incident occurred on Tuesday afternoon after approximately 50 migrants who had travelled from Normandy were taken to Dover for processing.

Thomas, founder of the Patriot Platform group, approached the dinghy in a yellow speedboat while broadcasting to more than 15,000 viewers. Video shows him pulling out a knife and slashing the inflatable hull as a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille Liberte remained aboard.

“This is English territory, it is not France anymore,” Thomas is heard shouting.

Thomas later said the purpose of his action was to ensure “that is one boat that won’t be used again.”

Tommy Robinson, the far-right activist whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon and a close associate of Thomas, claimed on social media that Thomas was arrested for attempting to “stop the invasion of our country”.

Thomas organised anti-immigration protests in Dover and Portsmouth in early September, which drew hundreds of demonstrators who blocked roads. He founded Patriot Platform earlier this year, rallying support for what he describes as “mass resistance” to “take our country back”.

Successive British governments have struggled to stop people – more than 41,000 last year – making the dangerous journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians, including Nigel Farage of the far-right party Reform UK, and has been used as a rallying point by anti-immigration activists.

articles.title: 'Jhoot ki goonj by frustrated leader': BJP mocks Rahul Gandhi's presser on EC-SIR row

articles.title: Americans lost over $20 billion to one type of crime. Here’s how we can fight it
articles.summary: Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet scams in 2025, with social media fraud costs eight times higher than 2020, FBI data reveals.
articles.body: Almost all kinds of crime, from homicide to car theft, are down, according to the latest FBI data. That’s great news, but one type of less-reported crime is up — way up. Americans reported losing $20.9 billion to internet-enabled crime in 2025, 26% higher than the year before and the highest figure ever recorded by the FBI. Folks over 60 reported $7.7 billion of it, averaging $38,500 apiece. The real toll is even higher, since the Federal Trade Commission notes that most victims never make a report. It’s clear more needs to be done to protect Americans from these crimes. But many of the losses aren’t hacks where a firewall was breached or a password stolen. They’re scams where victims are persuaded to voluntarily send money to overseas bad actors. That’s an important distinction because a transfer that the customer has been convinced to make looks to every automated system in the chain like a legitimate one. CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY The fact that the money leaves the country should also inform government’s response. Treasury estimates Americans lost at least $10 billion in 2024 to scam operations in Southeast Asia, a 66% increase. These are sophisticated operations in Burma, Cambodia and Laos, many staffed by trafficked workers held in debt bondage or via violence. Social media has shifted these scams into overdrive. The FTC reports scams originating on social platforms cost Americans $2.1 billion last year, eight times the 2020 figure, and more than any other contact method. Sadly, artificial intelligence (AI) is being utilized by these thieves so that they no longer need to have English proficiency or a real photograph. AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE Washington’s reflex for years was to try to force domestic institutions to cover the costs. In December 2024, the outgoing Biden Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued the operator of the Zelle payment network and three of its largest participating banks over scam losses. The suit was dismissed with prejudice three months later, which was the right outcome. American banks are already the most active force in the fight against both fraud and scams. Those institutions run real-time risk scoring on outbound payments, warn customers mid-transaction when money is headed to a new recipient and block transfers that trip their models — often while a customer insists the nice man from "the fraud department" is legitimate. NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS Banks have, at great expense, already proven to be key partners with law enforcement. Juniper Research estimates financial institutions spent roughly $21 billion on fraud prevention in 2025. Because of banks’ coordinated efforts with law enforcement, the FBI’s Financial Fraud Kill Chain froze $679 million of $1.16 billion in attempted theft last year. Further crackdowns on thieves cannot come from banks alone. Scams today begin long before the money transfer. Sophisticated scammers engage via social media, calls, texts and emails to establish rapport and manipulate victims. These criminals trick consumers, sometimes for an extended time and while impersonating a loved one, then banks only see the last step. A defense that begins at the payment screen is insufficient. Meanwhile, reimbursement mandates would raise the cost of banking and payment services on which tens of millions of households depend while leaving foreign criminals with their stolen funds to carry out more illicit activities against Americans. The thieves only care if their online wallets are frozen and bosses are indicted, not if banks get stuck with the tab. Fortunately, the source-focused approach has shown progress. In October, the U.S. and U.K. jointly sanctioned 146 individuals and entities tied to Cambodia’s Prince Group, DOJ indicted its chairman, and prosecutors moved to seize 127,271 Bitcoin — billions of dollars’ worth, the largest forfeiture in Justice Department history. The Scam Center Strike Force has seized over $401 million for return to victims, and the FBI’s Operation Level Up has warned more than 8,000 Americans mid-scam. FBI SEIZES RECORD-SETTING $8 BILLION IN CRYPTOCURRENCY AMID INTERCONTINENTAL 'SCAM COMPOUND' CRACKDOWN But today’s temporary measures enacted by executive orders need to be made permanent via statute, and private-sector partnerships expanded. Collaboration requires intelligence sharing while protecting customer privacy. Juniper Research estimates financial institutions spent roughly $21 billion on fraud prevention in 2025. Because of banks’ coordinated efforts with law enforcement, the FBI’s Financial Fraud Kill Chain froze $679 million of $1.16 billion in attempted theft last year. Joint analytics between telecommunications, social media, technology and banking firms with Treasury and FBI data would provide a network map no institution can see alone. Additionally, safe harbor clarifications would mean flagging suspicious activity isn’t itself a legal risk. WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE Scam syndicates should also be designated as terrorist organizations where they qualify, exposing their financiers to material-support charges and any foreign bank touching the money to secondary sanctions. Meanwhile, the State Department should attach diplomatic costs to hosting scam compounds. On the home front, telecom, tech and social media firms have a civic responsibility to American citizens to work more with Treasury, FTC and FCC in stopping criminals from preying on consumers. A basic first step for these companies is taking down fraudulent ads, instead of earning revenue from them at the expense of innocent consumers. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Congress, which has been conspicuously absent from this fight and derelict in duty, should raise penalties for cross-border scams, streamline extradition and give statutory footing to current executive orders so the crackdown on scammers survives beyond one administration. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The best results will come from stopping criminals before they’re able to communicate with innocent Americans, alongside a source-focused strategy that attacks where the money goes. The thief is not in Charlotte or San Francisco but in a compound on another continent. Until that thief is punished, there’s no incentive for the scams to stop, and Americans will keep paying, one grandmother’s savings at a time. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM E.J. ANTONI

articles.title: Nine Kazakh soldiers die in Caspian Sea training incident
articles.summary: Nine confirmed dead after 19 Kazakh soldiers swept out to sea during naval training in western Mangystau region.
articles.body:
Nine Kazakh military personnel have died after being swept out to sea during naval training exercises on the Caspian coast, the country’s Defence Ministry says.

The accident happened on Thursday in Kazakhstan’s western Mangystau region, which adjoins the Caspian Sea, during a combat training mission.

Nineteen personnel were swept out in total, according to preliminary information, and nine deaths have been confirmed so far, the ministry said in a statement posted on Telegram.

Three people have been rescued. A search and rescue operation for the remaining personnel was still under way, the ministry added.

The ministry said the accident was caused by a sudden deterioration in weather conditions.

The Caspian is bordered by Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan.

articles.title: Hurricane Polo brings fears of heavy rain and landslides in Mexico
articles.summary: Heavy rains could cause life-threatening flooding and landslides in Mexico, the US National Hurricane Center warned.
articles.body:
Hurricane Polo has sent heavy rain and strong waves across Mexico’s Pacific coast, while Tropical Storm Nolo is approaching Hawaii with the potential for catastrophic flooding.

Early on Thursday, the hurricane was swirling about 130 miles (209 kilometres) south-southwest of the Mexican city of Zihuatanejo. It was moving northwest at 7mph (11kph) and forecast to turn west-northwest later in the day, taking it further out to sea, before turning northwest on Saturday.

Polo was forecast to maintain Category 5 strength as it moves along Mexico’s coast over the next few days.

While the eye and the strongest winds were expected to remain at sea, the heavy rains could cause life-threatening flooding and landslides, warned the US National Hurricane Center in Miami.

A hurricane watch was issued for Hawaii county and disaster preparations are under way because Tropical Storm Nolo could hit the island on Friday or Saturday, warned the National Weather Service.

John Bravender, a weather service warning coordination meteorologist, said during a news conference on Wednesday afternoon that the tropical storm could develop into a major hurricane.

Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda told residents in a video message that they should start preparing for the storm. He urged them to put together emergency kits with food, water and medications, as well as trim vegetation and clear drains.

“This is a very serious situation,” he said. “We do believe that the rain is going to come. It’s coming already.”

Governor Josh Green’s office said public schools and state and county offices across Hawaii’s Big Island will close on Thursday and Friday, while Maui County will shut them on Friday ahead of the threat of heavy rain, winds and flooding.

articles.title: Tech industry group urges Trump administration to drop $103,265 H-1B fee proposal, asks how Silicon Valley will hire top talents
articles.summary: TechNet, an industry association representing major US technology companies, has urged the Trump administration to withdraw a proposed $103,265 fee on
articles.body: TechNet, an industry association representing major US technology companies, has urged the Trump administration to withdraw a proposed $103,265 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, saying the measure could make it harder for US companies to recruit highly skilled workers, Wall Street Journal reported. The group submitted comments to the Department of Homeland Security opposing the proposed fee. TechNet was joined in its comments by the Information Technology Industry Council and the Semiconductor Industry Association.The proposed fee comes as the administration is tightening the US high-skilled immigration system and encouraging employers to give greater priority to American workers. The proposal has drawn concern from technology companies that rely heavily on foreign-born workers, particularly for specialised positions in fields such as artificial intelligence, engineering and other STEM disciplines.TechNet said the proposed fee could undermine US competitiveness by making it more difficult for American companies to access specialised talent from around the world.“This proposal undermines the US global competitiveness championed by the President, preventing American companies from accessing the world's top talent -- talent that is central to driving innovation, launching businesses, and fostering prosperity in American communities,” the group said in its filing.TechNet's opposition comes as the technology industry and the Trump administration remain divided over high-skilled immigration. The industry group has previously called for expanding access to foreign talent while also supporting reforms aimed at preventing fraud and misuse of the H-1B programme. Its 2026 policy proposals specifically call for avoiding high H-1B fees that could discourage startups and small businesses from hiring foreign workers.New H-1B fee proposalThe Trump administration has proposed a new $103,265 fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, saying the charge would help the US government recover the costs of administering the country's legal immigration system.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), in its proposed rule, said the fee would apply to all H-1B petitions subject to the annual cap, including petitions eligible for the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption. The charge would be paid by the employer when the petition is filed and would come on top of other applicable H-1B fees.DHS said the proposal is intended to generate dedicated revenue to support immigration-related work carried out across several federal agencies, including US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), US Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of Labor, the Department of State and the Justice Department.The agency cited expenses including immigration adjudications, fraud detection, national-security vetting, information-technology modernization, records management, consular processing, immigration court proceedings and labor-related enforcement.DHS said it considered spreading the additional costs across a broader range of immigration applicants and petitioners but decided that doing so would impose additional costs on individuals whose applications may be less directly connected to employment-based immigration and who may have fewer resources to absorb higher fees.Instead, the agency proposed recovering the costs through H-1B cap-subject petitions, saying employers seeking to hire foreign skilled workers were a more appropriate group from which to recover the costs.The $103,265 figure was calculated by dividing an estimated $8.777 billion in costs by a projected 85,000 fee-paying H-1B petitions, producing a figure of about $103,264.57, which DHS rounded to $103,265.You use AI every day. articles.title: 19-year-old lost his lamp in an Australian cave in 1953, survived three days, became a NASA scientist; 68 years later, students found the lamp still hanging
articles.summary: Brian O’Brien was 19 when he entered the Yarrangobilly Caves in New South Wales in December 1953 with fellow caver Fred Stewart, but a short exploration
articles.body: Brian O’Brien was 19 when he entered the Yarrangobilly Caves in New South Wales in December 1953 with fellow caver Fred Stewart, but a short exploration turned into a three-day fight for survival. The pair became separated inside East Deep Cave, and O’Brien eventually lost the carbide lamp that was his only source of light after slipping and falling. He spent about 74 to 75 hours underground with little food and only a small amount of water before rescuers found him. O’Brien later became a NASA scientist and worked on lunar dust experiments carried aboard Apollo missions. His abandoned lamp remained inside the cave for decades. In 2021, two students discovered it about 60 metres underground, still hanging from a rocky ledge, before a volunteer caving team recovered it in 2026.A short cave trip turned into a 75-hour survival ordealO’Brien and Stewart were members of the Sydney University Speleological Society and had travelled to Yarrangobilly after finishing their university examinations. On December 15, 1953, they explored West Deep Creek Cave before deciding to have a quick look inside East Deep Creek Cave on their way back to camp. As their carbide lamps began running low, they started making their way towards the entrance, but O’Brien stayed behind to investigate another section. He became disoriented and was left alone in an unfamiliar part of the cave. His lamp eventually failed, leaving him in darkness. During his attempt to find a way out, he hooked the lamp onto a rock wall, then slipped and fell and could no longer locate it. He eventually heard rescuers after about 75 hours underground.The lost lamp remained in the cave for decadesO’Brien survived his ordeal, but the lamp stayed behind in the cave. For decades, it became a small but memorable part of his story, particularly because he continued to want it recovered. O’Brien's daughter, Ros O’Brien, told ABC that her father never stopped looking for the lamp and always wanted to bring it back. Brian O’Brien died in 2020 at the age of 86, meaning he did not live to see the object found. The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service later said the lamp remained undiscovered for more than 70 years, while the exact location of the object was eventually identified by a new generation of cavers.Two students spotted the lamp 68 years after it was lostThe lamp was finally spotted in 2021 by Brittany Meers and her friend Lachlan Bailey, who were students and exploring the cave as cavers. They found the relic roughly 60 metres underground, where it was hanging from a high ledge. At the time, they did not immediately understand its historical significance and left it in place. The discovery later became known within the caving community, prompting discussions about how it could be safely recovered while respecting the cave environment and the O’Brien family's wishes. The finding came 68 years after O’Brien had lost the lamp during his 1953 ordeal, creating the second chapter of a story that had begun more than six decades earlier.Volunteer cavers spent two hours reaching it in 2026Four volunteer cavers, including Meers, returned to the cave in 2026 to retrieve the lamp under a recovery mission coordinated with NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service. The route was difficult, with the team squeezing through narrow spaces and scrambling across challenging sections in temperatures that could fall to about 5 degrees Celsius. Although the lamp was only about 100 to 150 metres into the cave in a straight line, the obstacles made the journey considerably more difficult. After about two hours underground, the group reached the lamp and successfully removed it from the rock where it had remained since 1953. The object was reportedly in remarkably good condition, with surprisingly little corrosion after more than seven decades underground.The teenager became a NASA scientist and the lamp will now be displayedThe recovered lamp became an unexpected link between two very different parts of O’Brien's life. After surviving his cave ordeal, he went on to become a prominent space scientist specialising in lunar dust. An Australian government citation records that O’Brien served as a NASA principal investigator, invented the Apollo Dust Detector Experiment and developed experiments that were deployed on Apollo missions including Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15. His family has entrusted the recovered lamp to NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, which plans to preserve and display it at Yarrangobilly. Ros O’Brien and her son Bobby Cafagna travelled from Perth to witness the recovery, with the family describing the moment as a fitting end to a story that began when a 19-year-old became lost in the darknessYou use AI every day. articles.title: Has China received US F-35 parts by diverting an Australian shipment?
articles.summary: Australia and US investigate F-35 parts mistakenly sent to Hong Kong amid concerns over sensitive military technology.
articles.body:
The United States is investigating reports that parts of its advanced F-35 stealth fighter jet programme were diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the US.

The incident last week has prompted questions over whether China may have gained access to components of one of Washington’s most sophisticated weapons systems.

There has been no suggestion so far from US or Australian authorities that Beijing deliberately diverted the shipment or accessed the technology.

On Tuesday, Australia’s Defence Minister Richard Marles said the components involved were not “sensitive”. China’s Foreign Ministry says it was not aware of the incident.

So, what happened and how serious was this incident?

On Saturday, US media outlet Politico reported that a consignment of F-35 components, including a cockpit canopy designed with radar-deflecting technology and a weapons-bay door, was unexpectedly rerouted to Hong Kong after leaving Australia.

The Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Programme Office said it was aware of “a shipment issue” involving components from the fighter jet and was working with US authorities and industry partners to recover them.

“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.

Marles confirmed the incident and revealed that Australia was helping the US and Lockheed Martin, the F-35’s main contractor, to investigate what happened. “We are examining very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end,” he said. “Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”

Australia has 72 F-35s and is one of seven countries outside the US which share a global pool of spare parts. A warehouse at Williamtown, north of Sydney, serves as an Asia-Pacific hub supporting the warplanes.

Why was the shipment diverted to Hong Kong?

It is unclear. Neither the Pentagon nor Australian authorities have publicly explained why the shipment went to Hong Kong and there is no evidence showing that China was responsible for its diversion.

While Lockheed Martin manages the global spare-parts programme, two sources told the AFP news agency that the programme itself is controlled by the US military. Australian defence officials have previously said Canberra does not control or direct the export of F-35 components from the Williamtown warehouse.

Alex Gatopoulos, Al Jazeera’s defence editor, said the international nature of the programme makes its logistics somewhat complex.

“The F-35 programme, whilst American, is supplied by subcontractors from 11 countries. Thirteen countries, apart from the US, fly the F-35, so the logistics network supplying each air force is vast,” he said.

Lockheed Martin Australia declined to discuss specific shipping procedures for security reasons but said every shipment is handled with “utmost diligence” and in accordance with US regulations.

The incident is serious enough to warrant a Pentagon investigation to try to recover the components.

However, Australian Defence Minister Marles played down the security implications of the incident. “We’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts,” he said.

The concern stems from the F-35’s status as a fifth-generation stealth fighter incorporating stealth coatings, advanced radar, sensors and networking capabilities. More than 1,200 have been built, with 19 countries placing orders, according to the US Congressional Research Service.

China has also previously been accused of seeking information about the programme. A US Defense Science Board report released in 2013 alleged Chinese cyberattacks had accessed information from several Pentagon programmes, including the Joint Strike Fighter programme.

For years, US officials have warned about what they describe as an espionage threat from the Chinese state, while prosecutors have brought criminal cases against intelligence operatives from Beijing accused of stealing classified government material and proprietary commercial data, including via unlawful cyber intrusions.

In January, a former US Navy sailor received a prison term of more than 16 years after being found guilty of selling technical and operational manuals for vessels and naval systems to an intelligence officer acting on behalf of China.

However, Al Jazeera’s Defence Editor Alex Gatopoulos cautioned against assuming that possession of individual components would provide Beijing with any major technological advantages.

“Whilst China has a reputation for intense industrial espionage, its own stealth fighter jet programme is advanced, with sixth-generation prototypes coming online,” he said. “It’s debatable how much actual information China would glean from smaller, non-essential parts from an F-35.”

images.caption: A US Marine Corps F-35C on display at America's Air Show in San Diego, California, September 26, 2025 [Kevin Carter/Getty Images]
(Al Jazeera)

articles.title: Remains located, identified as missing Texas man Jason Landry
articles.summary: 21-year-old Jason Landry vanished in December 2020 while driving from San Marcos to his family’s home in Missouri City, Texas. His wrecked car was found abandoned on Salt Flat Road in Luling. His remains have now been located and identified.
articles.body: After nearly six years, one Texas family finally has some answers. On September 23, 2026, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s Cold Case Unit announced that “DNA analysis has conclusively identified recently recovered human remains as those of Jason Landry, who had been missing since December 13, 2020.” Jason, a 21-year-old Texas State University student, disappeared while driving home from San Marcos to visit family in Missouri City, Texas. Dateline featured his case in its “Missing in America” digital series in February 2021. Just after midnight on December 14, a volunteer fireman discovered Jason’s wrecked car abandoned on Salt Flat Road near Luling, Texas. The lights were still on, the keys were in the ignition and the front passenger side door was locked. But there was no sign of Jason. Jason’s father, Kent Landry, got a call from a state trooper at 2 a.m. telling him his son’s car had been found wrecked in a single-vehicle crash on the dark country road. “It’s a call that every parent fears,” Kent Landry told Dateline in 2021. “It’s our worst nightmare.” “Several of his personal belongings, including clothing, were found scattered near the crash site, but Landry was not located despite extensive searches by law enforcement, search teams, and volunteers,” the press release from the Texas AG states. Over the years, investigators conducted repeated searches and continued to review new leads. Then, on September 8, a local resident found human remains east of Salt Flat Road, between Soda Springs and Biggs Road, near the area where Jason vanished. “DNA testing conducted by the University of North Texas Center for Human Identification (“UNTCHI”) confirmed the remains belonged to Landry,” the press release stated. “The skeletal remains do not provide additional insight into the cause or manner of death, and investigators have found no indication of foul play.” “This development marks a critical moment in a case that has weighed heavily on our hearts for nearly six years. The Landry family has suffered an unimaginable tragedy, and they will remain in our prayers, especially during this incredibly difficult time,” Paxton said. “My Cold Case Unit will continue fighting to solve cases and bring closure on behalf of Texas families and victims.” The press release stated that Jason’s family has been notified and authorities are asking that their privacy be respected. articles.title: Israel offers cash to firms hit by trade ban; Europe dithers on new rules
articles.summary: Israel hopes to redirect goods from illegal Israeli settlements towards markets in Asia and South America.
articles.body:
The Israeli government plans to pay companies in illegal settlements up to 200,000 shekels ($54,000) following a commitment by European countries to ban their goods amid escalating human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Roey Fisher, head of Israel’s Foreign Trade Administration at the Ministry of Economy and Industry, told Israeli media outlet Calcalist that it has set up a “dedicated team” to help companies operating in illegal settlements find “alternative markets”, including the Philippines, India, the United Arab Emirates, Chile and Argentina. The assistance also covers exporters of fresh produce, and more than 25 applications for assistance have already been submitted by companies expected to be affected, the report added.

Fisher, however, played down the immediate reach of the bans. “Not everyone is boycotting us,” he told Calcalist, pointing to differences between European countries. “Right now, Spain and the Netherlands are among the only places in Europe where there is an effective boycott,” he said. “The countries that have announced boycotts, including England, have not applied them to all Israeli exports.”

Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera the grants would provide a “significant lift” for exporters seeking new markets, but said the financial impact of the bans remained “uncertain”. She said the grants were unlikely to fully offset lost sales in the short term, with the UK and EU together accounting for “over a third of Israel’s exports”.

But Norman said the government support highlighted a broader challenge for countries seeking to economically target settlements. “The question of the grants highlights the challenge for states like the UK or European states when trying to target the settlements, when the settlements themselves are still supported by the Israeli government,” she said.

Shamiul Joarder, director at Friends of Al-Aqsa, a UK-based nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that government support helping exporters find alternative markets could “cushion the commercial impact” of the bans. “This demonstrates why targeting settlement goods alone is insufficient, as the settlement economy can simply redirect its trade elsewhere,” he added.

Which import bans are actually in force?

While a growing number of countries have pledged to restrict trade with Israeli settlements, far fewer have actually put those measures into force. On September 8, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom issued a joint statement saying they intended to introduce national restrictions, support restrictions at the European level or were considering such measures.

But among those countries, only a handful have enacted restrictions. Spain and Ireland have introduced measures targeting imports of settlement goods, while the Netherlands brought its ban into force on September 22.

The Dutch measure goes further than some others. It prohibits the import, purchase and sale of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory, as well as services facilitating that trade and attempts to circumvent the restrictions. Its significance also extends beyond the Dutch market, with the Netherlands serving as a major gateway for goods entering the rest of Europe.

Elsewhere, measures remain at various stages and are not yet operational. Belgium’s cabinet approved a draft measure on July 18 that would systematically refuse import permits for goods identified as coming from Israeli settlements. But the proposal includes a 120-day transition period and was sent to the Council of State for an opinion, meaning cabinet approval alone did not bring it into force.

Norway has put forward draft legislation that would go further than an import ban, prohibiting both imports from and exports to illegal Israeli settlements. But the legislation has yet to enter into force, with the Norwegian government listing it as still under consideration.

France and Canada have pledged national measures that have yet to take effect. Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden signed the joint statement, but none has announced that a national ban on settlement goods has entered into force. Sweden has instead proposed restrictions at the EU level, including higher tariffs on settlement goods and new export-certificate requirements.

Meanwhile, in the UK, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the legislation would be introduced within six to nine months, leaving a gap between the government’s pledge and any ban taking legal effect.

Norman said the UK’s six-to-nine-month timetable could give officials time to work through the practical details of implementing the ban. “I think that is to just work out logistics, and for UK firms to adapt so they don’t hurt their own domestic businesses,” she said.

The delay could also allow the government to wait for Israel’s elections, she added, “and see what the outcome is there, and how a new government approaches settlement expansion”.

Even in the United States, Israel’s closest ally, a group of senators has introduced a separate bill seeking sanctions against people involved in constructing Israel’s E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank. It remains a proposal rather than a trade restriction in force.

But Israeli media reports suggest the country also sees the US as a potential avenue for relief should the import bans come into force, with lobbyists reportedly pushing for sanctions relief. There have also been warnings that the bans could trigger sanctions from US states under anti-boycott legislation.

articles.title: Taliban govt says Pakistan strikes kill 4 civilians in Afghanistan
articles.summary: Afghanistan's Taliban government said on Thursday that Pakistani airstrikes on several provinces had killed four civilians, days after another deadly bombard...
articles.body:
Afghanistan's Taliban government said on Thursday that Pakistani airstrikes on several provinces had killed four civilians, days after another deadly bombardment and a militant attack in Pakistan.

The latest targets included the southern province of Kandahar, seat of the Taliban government's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada.

Islamabad's information minister said Pakistani forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan -- without specifying where -- accusing its neighbour of allowing "terrorist sanctuaries" on its soil.

Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in a post on X that "the Pakistani military regime once again committed aggression and conducted aerial bombardments against Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces".

"Four civilians were martyred in this criminal act of aggression," he added, vowing to deliver an "appropriate response".

The foreign ministry said it had summoned Pakistan's charge d'affaires in Kabul to protest "the issue of the violation of Afghanistan's airspace and the Pakistani army's airstrikes on a number of the country's provinces".

The raids come days after a deadly bombardment in eastern Afghanistan and nearly a week after a militant attack on a police headquarters in northern Pakistan that killed at least 31 people.

A Kandahar resident told AFP on Thursday they heard a jet, then a large explosion, followed by a fire in the centre of the city.

Hours later, Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar confirmed "precision aerial and drone strikes", in a post on X.

"The strikes were deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan," he said.

At least three civilians were killed in the strikes on eastern Afghanistan earlier this week, the United Nations reported. Pakistan said 28 militants had been killed.

On Thursday, local officials told AFP that Pakistan had struck eastern Afghan provinces overnight.

In Paktia, jets bombed the Afghan army's 203rd Mansouri Corps, said the provincial governor's spokesman Mohammad Rasool Ahmadi, without providing any information on casualties.

Airstrikes also targeted Khost province without causing casualties, said Mustaghfa Gurbaz, the governor's spokesman there.

Salamat Khan, 66, the landlord of a damaged house in Khost, told AFP there had been "no military, no militants" in the building.

While violence has repeatedly flared in the border area, strikes on Afghan cities are rare.

Both Kandahar and the capital Kabul were hit when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war in late February, with weeks of violence killing hundreds of Afghan civilians, according to the UN mission UNAMA.

The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.

UNAMA said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.

Security issues have proved a sticking point in any push for de-escalation, especially Pakistan's demand that Afghanistan curb the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militant group.

Islamabad accuses the Taliban government of sheltering militants behind a surge in attacks, particularly the TTP, which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years.

"For years, Pakistan has repeatedly conveyed its grave concerns to the Afghan Taliban regime and its interlocutors regarding the continued presence of terrorist sanctuaries and their support networks on Afghan soil," Tarar said on X Thursday.

"Instead of dismantling these networks... the Afghan Taliban regime has chosen to escalate the situation through hostile drone operations against Pakistan."

Afghan officials deny the charge and counter that Pakistan harbours hostile groups and does not respect its sovereignty.

A group linked to the TTP has claimed the attack on a police headquarters in northern Pakistan on Friday that killed at least 31 people.

articles.title: In 2017, this man got a bank job; 8 years later, he returned to his family in Andhra Pradesh after his father's death and started farming again; he now earns Rs 5,000 daily from vegetables
articles.summary: When Ravuri Sekhar joined Andhra Bank in 2017, his family was happy to see him begin a career in banking.
articles.body: When Ravuri Sekhar joined Andhra Bank in 2017, his family was happy to see him begin a career in banking. While he worked at the bank, his parents continued managing their five-acre family farm in Chennam Raju Palli village in Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh. That changed in 2025 after the death of his father, Nageswara Rao. “However, when my father (Nageswara Rao) passed away in 2025, I decided to quit my job and return home to take care of my family and farm,” Sekhar told 30Stades in an interview.Returning to the farm also meant changing the way it was cultivated. Sekhar decided not to depend on chemical fertilisers and pesticides and moved away from the family's earlier cultivation of pulses and paddy. Instead, he adopted a multi-cropping model. The farm now combines long-term crops such as avocado, coconut and mahogany with shorter-duration vegetable crops.Growing vegetables between long-term cropsSekhar has planted avocado across two acres, while another one-and-a-half acres is being used for coconut and mahogany, as reported by 30Stades. The trees are meant to provide income over different time periods. Avocado and coconut are expected to start fruiting in another two to three years, while the mahogany trees are expected to provide timber returns in around 12 to 15 years. Rather than leave the space between the young trees unused, Sekhar uses it for vegetable cultivation. His vegetable crops include tomato, okra, brinjal, cluster beans, cucumber, chilli, carrot, turmeric, beetroot and cauliflower.Farm produces over 100 kg of vegetables dailyAccording to 30Stades, the farm currently produces more than 100 kg of vegetables a day. Because the farm is located alongside a highway, some customers buy the vegetables directly from the farm. Sekhar also sells the produce at the local mandi. He said the response from customers has encouraged him to continue with the model. “Consumers who purchase the vegetables once return to buy them again due to their quality and taste,” Sekhar told 30Stades. The selling price varies by crop. Tomatoes are sold for around Rs 40 per kg, while okra sells for about Rs 60 per kg and brinjal for around Rs 50 per kg. “The average is around Rs 50 per kg, which leads to a daily income of around Rs 5,000,” Sekhar said, according to 30Stades.Why he moved away from chemical inputsSekhar's father had earlier used conventional chemical fertilisers and pesticides on the farm. For Sekhar, the rising cost of agricultural inputs became one reason to look for another approach. The farm now uses natural inputs prepared on the property. One of them is ‘Jeevamrutha,’ made using cow dung, cow urine, pulse flour and jaggery. These inputs are applied to the soil and crops, including through irrigation and spraying. “I also use Ghana Jeevamrutha and other inputs made on the farm,” Sekhar said.Natural methods for pest managementSekhar has also adopted methods to manage pests without depending entirely on chemical pesticides. “We use several pest-management techniques, including bird perches and yellow sticky traps,” he told 30Stades. Bird perches encourage insect-eating birds to visit the field, while yellow sticky traps are used to monitor and control certain insect pests. “These techniques are part of an integrated approach to crop protection,” Sekhar said, according to 30Stades.Sekhar also focuses on soil health. He points to the relationship between the soil's carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and microbial activity. When biological activity in soil declines, nutrient deficiencies and pest and disease problems can increase, potentially raising cultivation costs. articles.title: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
articles.summary: The suspect is alleged to have been an accessory to murder at the Stalag 326 camp, where tens of thousands of Soviet PoWs died.
articles.body:
German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.

The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.

A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.

That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.

No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.

More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.

But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.

One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region.

Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.

Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

The prosecutor made clear the investigation surrounding the 105-year-old was still under way and that the allegations of being an accessory to multiple murders related to his activities at Stalag 36.

There has been no statute of limitations in Germany for either murder or accessory to murder since 1979, to enable the prosecution of Nazi-era crimes.

Another centenarian camp guard from the Hemer Stalag VI A camp is also said to be under investigation.

However, bringing perpetrators to justice more than 80 years after the war is now fraught with difficulty.

Four years ago a 101-year-old concentration camp guard was given a five-year jail term for complicity in murder at Sachsenhausen. Josef Schütz was the oldest Nazi criminal ever brought to justice.

He never served time in jail and died in 2023 while appealing his sentence.

A former Nazi concentration camp secretary was convicted in 2022 of abetting murder and given a suspended jail term. She died last year aged 99.

Although prosecution of Nazi crimes is handled by the public prosecutors in the western city of Dortmund, cases are initially taken on by the central office for Nazi crime investigations in Ludwigsburg in the south-west.

articles.title: 87-year-old’s eviction in Madrid sparks protests as Spain's housing crisis deepens
articles.summary: For 87-year-old Maricarmen, a home she had lived in for 70 years became unaffordable after the real estate firm that owned her apartment raised her
articles.body: For 87-year-old Maricarmen, a home she had lived in for 70 years became unaffordable after the real estate firm that owned her apartment raised her monthly rent by 275%.Her eviction from the Madrid property on Wednesday, carried out as she was taken away on a stretcher, has now become a focal point in Spain's long-running housing crisis.The eviction, broadcast live on television, drew protesters who surrounded Maricarmen as police escorted her from the property.According to news agency AFP, Thousands later took to the streets in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities, protesting both her eviction and housing costs that have increasingly put homes beyond the reach of renters and buyers.The episode has also intensified a political dispute over Spain's housing policies ahead of next year's general election.Housing costs rise as affordable supply remains limitedHousing costs have increased sharply across Spain over the past decade. The average price of a square metre for both rental and purchase properties has risen by around 50%, according to real estate portal Idealista and official figures.Madrid has been particularly affected by rising prices. The city has topped a global ranking for luxury properties compiled by real estate firm Barnes for two consecutive years.The housing pressure extends beyond the luxury segment. Spain's consumer group OCU said finding an apartment in Madrid or Barcelona for less than 700 euros a month had become "extremely difficult" and called for more affordable rental housing.A major issue is the limited size of Spain's public housing stock. Only 1.2% of the country's housing stock is publicly owned, according to OECD figures. The proportion is substantially lower than in countries including Britain, France and the Netherlands.Residents have also blamed short-term tourist rentals such as Airbnb for pushing up prices and reducing the supply of homes available to residents. The issue has prompted large protests in popular tourist destinations including Barcelona.Investment funds have also faced criticism from housing campaigners, who refer to some of them as "vulture funds" and accuse them of prioritising profits over affordability.Maricarmen's eviction becomes political flashpointThe eviction has quickly become part of Spain's political debate, with parties preparing their positions ahead of next year's general election.Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez blamed the conservative-run Madrid city and regional authorities for their role in the eviction and described it as an unacceptable "social tragedy".The Madrid region's Popular Party leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso rejected the criticism, accusing the national government of "demagoguery" and saying it had "not done anything" during Sanchez's eight years in office.The dispute reflects the division of responsibilities over housing in Spain. While the leftist national government has spent years seeking to reform the housing market, regional authorities hold much of the power over housing policy.Guillermo Fernandez Vazquez, a professor at Madrid's Carlos III University, told AFP that the incident had again exposed what he described as the failure and "powerlessness" of housing policies.In a context of "inflation and loss of purchasing power", he said, the situation did not benefit any political party.Government pushes for eviction law as coalition faces pressureSanchez has called on parliament to pass legislation that would prohibit such evictions. However, his coalition does not have a majority and the incident has already exposed strains within the governing alliance.Far-left coalition partner Sumar has called for a rent freeze and the expropriation of Maricarmen's former home.Her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told public broadcaster RTVE that there was currently "no legal umbrella that enables the suspension of the eviction of vulnerable people".She said protections introduced through royal decrees had repeatedly served as temporary measures but were ultimately "sticking plasters and insufficient".The political debate is also unfolding against a separate controversy involving Ayuso and a luxury Madrid penthouse that she allegedly acquired with public money. Ayuso denies wrongdoing.According to Fernandez Vazquez, the Popular Party will also want to move beyond that controversy as quickly as possible.For Spain's housing market, however, Maricarmen's eviction has brought together several of the issues at the centre of the crisis — rising rents, limited public housing, pressure from investment and tourism, and disagreements between national and regional authorities over how to respond.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: 'No obligations under Rome Statute for overflights': France defends not arresting Netanyahu
articles.summary: France has defended its decision not to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu despite an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant against him.
articles.body: France has defended its decision not to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu despite an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant against him.Netanyahu’s plane crossed French airspace on Thursday en route to the United Nations. As a signatory to the ICC’s founding Rome Statute, France is formally bound to cooperate with the court, including by arresting suspects who enter its territory.French foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux told reporters the clearance to Netanyahu's aircraft was "in full conformity with international law.""The Rome Statute does not impose any obligations regarding overflights of its territory by a state plane which has a passenger who is targeted by an arrest warrant," Confavreux said.According to flight-tracking app Flightradar24, Netanyahu’s plane flew over Greece, Italy and France. An Italian foreign ministry spokesperson said they could not immediately confirm whether Israel had sought permission for the overflight.Netanyahu faces restrictions on travel to several countries because of an ICC arrest warrant issued against him and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, as well as a separate warrant for a former Hamas military commander, in 2024.Last year, Netanyahu took a circuitous route to New York to avoid the airspace of several European countries, including France, according to media reports.Israel rejects the ICC’s jurisdiction and denies committing war crimes in Gaza. It says its military campaign was aimed at eliminating Hamas following the group’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Israel is contesting the warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant.The United States, a close Israeli ally and non-signatory to the Rome Statute, has launched a campaign to isolate the court. President Donald Trump this week urged members of The Hague-based court to leave what he called an “out of control institution”. France has condemned threats against the ICC.Netanyahu was making a brief visit to the US to address world leaders at the UN General Assembly and was expected to return to Israel later on Thursday.(With Reuters inputs)You use AI every day. articles.summary: GREATER NOIDA: The drivers of the sleeper bus that caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway, killing nine passengers, on Thursday denied allegations that they
articles.body: GREATER NOIDA: The drivers of the sleeper bus that caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway, killing nine passengers, on Thursday denied allegations that they were smoking inside the vehicle or ignored warnings about smoke.The bus, meanwhile, had nine pending traffic challans in Delhi, mostly for overspeeding and improper parking, news agency ANI reported.Three accused, including two drivers and a conductor, were sent to jail by a local court on Thursday in connection with the fire.While being escorted from the court, the drivers denied passengers’ allegations that they had been smoking beedis or cigarettes inside the bus.“We do not smoke at all. We never smoke beedis or cigarettes. These allegations are completely false,” one of the drivers said.Asked if passengers had alerted them about a burning smell or smoke, he said, “No, that is completely incorrect. Nothing of that sort was told to us.”The second driver also denied consuming tobacco products and said he suspected that an electrical malfunction had triggered the fire. “It seems a short circuit caused the fire,” he said, ANI reported.The bus’s traffic record also came under scrutiny after DCP Traffic (Central Range) K Ramesh said the vehicle had nine pending challans in Delhi, mostly for overspeeding and improper parking.Ramesh said the bus had a valid permit until October 26 and that traffic police regularly inspect vehicles for permit violations and mandatory safety equipment, including fire extinguishers.He said existing rules do not allow a vehicle to be impounded solely for unpaid challans, though recent amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules have introduced provisions to restrict certain services for persistent defaulters.The officer added that buses operating without a valid permit or those whose drivers do not meet the mandatory five-year driving experience requirement could be impounded, ANI reported.Nine killed in Yamuna Expressway bus fireThe sleeper bus was travelling from Kashmiri Gate in New Delhi to Mahoba when it caught fire near the 33-kilometre milestone of the Yamuna Expressway around 11.30pm on September 23.According to the FIR registered at Jewar police station, around 30-35 passengers were travelling on the bus.Some passengers reportedly noticed a burning smell from the driver’s cabin and alerted the driver and conductor. The FIR alleges that they did not stop the bus immediately and continued smoking inside the cabin.The fire then spread rapidly through the vehicle, trapping several passengers inside, ANI reported.Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced an ex-gratia of Rs 2 lakh from the PMNRF for the next of kin of each of the nine deceased and Rs 50,000 for each injured passenger.Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath also announced Rs 2 lakh for each deceased victim’s family and Rs 50,000 for the injured.The three accused were produced before a local court on Thursday and sent to jail as the investigation into the cause of the fire and the circumstances surrounding the deaths continued.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: From red carpet to flypast to banquet, Trump lays it on thick for Xi
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: If diplomacy is the art of keeping a straight face, China’s leader Xi Jinping won hands down during the opening act on
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: If diplomacy is the art of keeping a straight face, China’s leader Xi Jinping won hands down during the opening act on Thursday at Andrews Air Force Base where US President Donald Trump received him on a state visit.For a fleeting moment, the changing balance of the US-China relationship was captured not in a joint communique, but in a visual metaphor. As American bombers roared overhead in a flypast intended to wow the visitor, it was Trump who winced, while Xi watched impassively -- an unintended piece of geopolitical choreography more eloquent than any statement.Beyond those few revealing seconds, there were other cues that pointed to the new phase of the relationship that indicated China is seen as a peer, even as some pundits believe it is starting to eclipse America. The Chinese president received something few recalled in living memory -- a planeside red carpet welcome that saw Trump himself waiting at the foot of the stairway, a presidential gesture so rare that historians recalled Prez Kennedy welcoming British PM Harold Macmillan at an airport in 1962 as the last comparable instance.“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit - Better than ever. Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL! “ Trump said later on his social media platform, laying it on thick. All this is remarkable coming from a man who roasted Barack Obama in 2012 for giving then Xi a ceremonial welcome. “So wrong! @BarackObama is hosting China's VP Xi Jinping today at the Pentagon with a full honor ceremony with music and cannons…” Trump had tweeted.And Washington did not merely roll out the red carpet. It literally measured it, ironed it and, according to one wag, made sure Xi’s shoes would not gather any dust. It also announced that the two sides have agreed to extend their trade truce till January, removing at least one immediate irritant before the summit, despite Trump having signed a bill that will empower him to impose100 percent tariff on countries -- notably China and India -- buying Russian energy.More pomp and pageantry is to follow over the next 48 hours with a ceremonial welcome at the White House followed by a banquet and a private tea party involving the first couples. In fact, Trump appears so anxious to court China that he has even deployed First Lady Melania Trump – who has maintained a relatively low public profile for long stretches of the second Trump presidency – for a starring diplomatic role. She was at the airbase with Trump and will host Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan separately, including a visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art. On Friday, the presidential couples are scheduled for private tea before visiting the National Archives, where they will review archival material on US-China ties.The First Lady herself offered the philosophy behind the extravaganza on Fox & Friends, saying, “He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect.” The White House later released details of Thursday’s banquet, revealing that the First Lady led the preparations for the dinner. On the menu, “American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together” – including a toast of Schramsberg "Blanc De Noir," honoring the historic “Toast to Peace” shared by President Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing in 1972.Not everyone from the Trump universe is in tune with the over-the-top welcome. “China should be held accountable for disrespecting President Trump and our country. For stealing an election. For murdering 1.2 million Americans. For helping Iran kill American service members,” raged Laura Loomer, a Trump whisperer who has the President’s ear, fuming that “the hospitality is way more than Xi deserves.” But a more sobering perspective came from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who asserted that it would be irresponsible not to engage Beijing at the highest level despite differences. “The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century,” Rubio said, echoing words that the US till recently had used for its ties with India, which is probably watching the scenario with consternation.Still, there are many skeptics in the global commentariat who think Trump may have overplayed the welcome.”Greeting him personally is a real gamble, because Trump spent his own leverage before the talking started, and the list he needs to work through is long: fentanyl, tariffs, chips, rare earths, and China's role in both Ukraine and Iran,” noted popular podcast host Mario Nawfal. “If he (Xi) walks away from three days of pageantry without a single commitment, Beijing got the photographs for free,” he added.You use AI every day. articles.title: Glasgow City Council to fire and re-hire over 23,000 employees
articles.summary: It says redundancy notices will be withdrawn if the three unions agree to ballot their members on the pay offer.
articles.body:
Glasgow City Council is to sack more than 23,000 members of staff and then rehire them to new contracts after pay talks broke down with unions.

The local authority says letters will be sent to its non-teaching staff next week, with new contracts then taking effect from 1 January.

Talks earlier this week between the council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart on Wednesday when Unison said it would not ballot its members on a proposed new pay offer.

The negotiations concerned plans by the council to implement a new pay and grading system, to replace one that was found to discriminate against mostly women workers. However the move meant 11% of employees would see wages cut.

The council said redundancy notices would be withdrawn if the three unions agreed to ballot their members on the pay offer.

The letters of dismissal will cover every member of non-teaching staff on the council's books, including chief executive Susanne Millar, nursery staff and refuse collectors.

Unions called the move a "scandalous threat" and demanded it be withdrawn.

Glasgow City Council at 'critical' point over £110m budget gap

Glasgow City Council approves plan to cut pay for some workers

Hundreds of council workers face wages cut in end to equal pay row

In a statement, the council's director of communications and corporate governance Colin Edgar claimed Unison had betrayed its own members by not balloting them.

He said talks breaking down meant there was now "no agreed way forward between the council and the joint trade unions".

"The council has gone as far as it can," said Edgar. "The new pay and grading scheme removes unequal pay and sees pay rise or stay the same for 90% of staff – the council's total pay bill will be substantially higher.

"For those staff who are in detriment our joint trade unions negotiated an increase in pay protection from six months to 12 months.

"Additionally, some trade unions are devoting energy to local consultations to mitigate the impact on those colleagues in detriment – focusing on providing specific solutions."

Edgar said council officials hoped to meet with Unison earlier but the union had not attended the meeting.

He added: "The offer which has been unilaterally rejected by Unison would have taken dismissals off the table and seen additional cash for those members of staff, and members of all unions, who are due back pay.

"It beggars belief that they would betray their own members in this way."

Unison Scotland regional organiser Mandy McDowall said: "Glasgow City Council staff are not going to be bounced into a shoddy deal by bosses trying to bully them with arbitrary deadlines.

"The council's decision to dismiss workers helps nobody and Glasgow City Council risks being labelled a pariah employer if it refuses to negotiate in good faith with its staff."

She added Unison would continue to work to secure a fair deal and would ballot its members on an offer once discussions had finished.

Graham McNabb, an industrial officer with Unite the Union, said: "Glasgow City Council must remove direct threats to our membership in its proposed new pay and grading structure, whether it is through cuts to terms and conditions, or the scandalous threat of fire and rehire tactics.

"If they go down this reckless path then it will be met with the full force of Unite."

At a meeting last month, the council agreed to an overhaul of its pay and grading structure after eight years of negotiations.

The new system would see 63% of those affected gain financially while 11% will have their wages reduced.

The highest drop in wages is expected to be around £11,500.

The GMB and Unite had earlier said they secured an additional £110m into the funding package to resolve key issues affecting "the vast majority of our members".

The two unions sent out a message to staff earlier warning the fire and rehire policy might be introduced, and saying the extra money was now "hanging by a thread."

However Unison said this extra funding would go towards towards "assimilation and arrears", and not help the staff facing wage cuts.

GMB and Unite both wanted the council to table the offer so members could make a decision.

Both unions stated that if the council pursues the fire and rehire policy then they will "immediately enter into dispute to secure the improved package and halt fire and rehire".

A letter to members of GMB and Unite, sent before the council announced it was implementing the policy, stated fire and re-hire would be a "self-defeating step" by the local authority.

It added that such a move would "hasten a prolonged industrial dispute" between unions and the council.

The letters sent to staff say their new contracts would begin the day after the old ones would end, and that continuity of service would not be affected.

Glasgow City Council has been embroiled in problems over pay for years.

The local authority previously paid out about £770m after it emerged female workers in roles such as catering or cleaning had for years been receiving up to £3 an hour less than those in male-dominated areas such as refuse collection.

The new job evaluation scheme was designed to draw a line under the row by bringing pay scales into line with equality law, but it also meant some staff would face wage cuts, depending on what pay banding the new scheme placed them in.

This is a major escalation of the row over the proposed new pay structure at Glasgow City Council.

So-called "fire and rehire" tactics are always controversial. Unions often associate them with private sector companies seeking cuts - not major public sector employers.

Glasgow City Council had previously said it would explore mitigations for the 11% of staff facing a pay cut.

If the unions agree to ballot their members on the pay structure, the threat of "fire and rehire" will be withdrawn.

It is worth stressing that nobody is simply facing the sack as such. However anyone who did not sign a new contract would not have a job. Someone facing a pay cut may attempt to claim constructive dismissal.

Unions are likely to fight Glasgow City Council's plan vigorously. Industrial action cannot be ruled out if there is no amicable settlement.

articles.title: Criticised AI mural of Bristol on Bedminster pub wall removed
articles.summary: The AI-generated mural was in a part of the city which hosts Europe's largest street art festival.
articles.body:
A controversial mural which was generated by AI and plastered on the wall of a city pub has been removed.

The vinyl sticker, which was put on the side of the Jolly Colliers pub in Bedminster, Bristol, on Wednesday featured iconic symbols of the city such as hot air balloons and the Clifton Suspension Bridge.

The mural, which was located in the part of the city that hosts Europe's largest street art festival Upfest, was removed earlier.

A spokesperson for Punch Pubs & Co, which owns the pub, said it had nothing to add to a previous statement in which it said the mural was a "temporary solution" which they were working with local artists to replace.

articles.title: Panda diplomacy: Xi announces 2 giant pandas for Atlanta zoo in US
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping brought a softer touch to his meeting with US President Donald Trump and other White House officials on Thursday, announcing
articles.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping brought a softer touch to his meeting with US President Donald Trump and other White House officials on Thursday, announcing that two giant pandas would soon head to Atlanta as an “envoy of friendship”.The announcement was the latest development in a new panda conservation agreement between the Atlanta zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association. Under the agreement, male panda Ping Ping and female panda Fu Shuang are expected to arrive from the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding."We can't wait to meet Ping Ping and Fu Shuang and to welcome our members, guests, city, and community back to the wonder and joy of giant pandas," Atlanta zoo president Raymond B. King said in a statement in April.China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the new conservation cooperation would help improve the health and well-being of giant pandas, promote global biodiversity protection and strengthen friendship between the Chinese and American people.Atlanta's earlier panda agreement with China, which ended in 2024, saw pandas Lun Lun and Yang Yang produce seven cubs, according to the zoo. The pair and their two youngest offspring left Atlanta for China in October 2024, while their other offspring were already in China.There is no confirmed date yet for Ping Ping and Fu Shuang's arrival in Atlanta. A zoo spokesperson told CBS News Atlanta that the date would not be disclosed for now.Meanwhile, the zoo is carrying out facility upgrades and other preparations to make the pandas' new home safer and more comfortable, with technical guidance from Chinese experts.Pandas have long been more than a popular attraction in the US-China relationship. Beijing gifted a pair to the National Zoo in Washington, DC, in 1972, making the animals a lasting symbol of friendship between the two countries.China has also used its giant panda loan programme as an instrument of soft-power diplomacy around the world. The policy is famously known as "panda diplomacy"Two US zoos currently have pandas. The National Zoo and the San Diego Zoo both received pandas from China in 2024.You use AI every day.
